entry: Dutch professional [[Association football|football]] club based in [[Amsterdam]]. Founded in 1900, Ajax holds the national records for 36 [[Eredivisie]] titles and 20 KNVB Cups. It was one of the most successful clubs of the 20th century, completing the continental treble in 1972 by winning the Eredivisie, the KNVB Cup and the European Cup. The club is known for developing young players through its youth academy.

Period of rapid growth in [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] beginning in the mid-2010s and accelerating in the 2020s. Generative models, especially [[Large language model|large language models]] that produce text and code, drove much of the growth. Leading proprietary models have come from companies including Anthropic and OpenAI, and from divisions of Google and Meta, while Chinese companies have favored open-weight releases. The boom has raised concerns about energy use, copyright, deepfakes and a possible economic bubble. Some observers, including Kai-Fu Lee, describe an AI arms race between the U.S. and China. In the second quarter of 2026, [[Nvidia]] was the world's largest company by market capitalization.

[[Soviet Union|Soviet]] 7.62×39mm [[Assault rifle|assault rifle]]. Designed by Mikhail Kalashnikov, the AK-47 was accepted by the Soviet Armed Forces in 1949 and became the basis of the Kalashnikov family of rifles. Its reliability in harsh conditions, low production cost and ease of use made it popular worldwide. It was used by [[Warsaw Pact]] forces as well as by irregular forces and insurgencies. As of 2004, about 100 million of an estimated 500 million firearms worldwide belonged to the Kalashnikov family, three-quarters of them AK-47s.

Rare, terminal neurodegenerative disease, also called motor neuron disease (MND). ALS causes progressive loss of the motor neurons that control voluntary muscles, until a patient cannot eat, speak, move or breathe without support. Death usually results from [[Respiratory failure|respiratory failure]]. Most cases (about 90–95%) have no known cause; about 5–10% are familial, most often linked to mutations in the C9orf72 gene. Riluzole and edaravone slow progression, but there is no cure. Average survival from onset is two to four years, and about 10% of patients survive more than ten years.

American multinational [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] company headquartered in Santa Clara, California. AMD designs [[Central processing unit|central processing units]] (CPUs), graphics processors and field-programmable gate arrays for personal computers, gaming, data centers and embedded systems. Founded in 1969 by Jerry Sanders and colleagues from Fairchild Semiconductor, it entered the microprocessor market in 1975 by reverse-engineering [[Intel]]'s 8080. A cross-license agreement allowed AMD to build x86 clones of Intel processors from 1981. Its Ryzen processors regained market share in the late 2010s. In 2022 AMD surpassed Intel in market capitalization for the first time and acquired Xilinx.

American web portal and former online service provider, based in New York City and owned by Bending Spoons. AOL grew from the Quantum Link online service and became the largest U.S. online service in the mid-1990s. It pioneered chat rooms and instant messaging, and it once provided [[Internet|Internet access]] to millions of dial-up customers. In 1998 AOL bought Netscape for US$4.2 billion. In 2001 it acquired Time Warner in the largest merger in U.S. history. Its decline followed the rise of broadband, and it was merged with [[Yahoo]] after Verizon acquired it in 2015.

Type of software interface that connects [[Computer program|computer programs]] or computers with one another. Unlike a [[User interface|user interface]], which connects a computer to a person, an API is used by programmers and other software. It hides a system's internal details, exposing only the parts a programmer needs, so the internals can change without breaking the connection. Web APIs allow computers joined by the [[Internet]] to communicate; common styles include REST, SOAP and GraphQL. APIs originated in the 1940s, but the term did not emerge until the 1960s and 1970s.

Family of RISC instruction set architectures for computer processors. Arm Holdings develops the architecture and licenses it to companies that build chips, as well as licensing processor cores. Low power consumption and low heat output make ARM processors common in [[Smartphone|smartphones]], laptops and embedded systems. They are also used in servers and in Fugaku, the world's fastest [[Supercomputer|supercomputer]] from 2020 to 2022. Over 230 billion ARM chips have been produced since at least 2003, making ARM the most widely used family of instruction set architectures.

Early packet-switched [[Computer network|computer network]], established by the Advanced Research Projects Agency (now DARPA) of the [[United States Department of Defense|U.S. Department of Defense]]. Bob Taylor initiated the project in 1966, and the first computers were connected in 1969. The network was declared operational in 1971 and supported remote login, file transfer and an early form of [[Email|email]]. It was among the first networks to use the TCP/IP protocol suite, which became the technical foundation of the [[Internet]]. Version 4 of TCP/IP was installed on 1 January 1983. ARPANET was formally decommissioned in 1990.

[[Character encoding]] standard that represents 128 code points using seven-bit values from 0 to 127. Its 95 printable characters include the digits 0–9, English letters and common punctuation; its 33 control codes originated with teleprinters. ASCII was first published in 1963 as ASA X3.4-1963. It has no code points for diacritical marks, so it does not directly support words such as résumé. The first 128 code points of [[Unicode]] are identical to ASCII, and the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority prefers the name US-ASCII.

Intergovernmental forum of all 11 states in Southeast Asia, founded in 1967 by five countries. ASEAN focuses on economic development, peaceful coexistence and adherence to international norms. It operates by consensus and respects national [[Sovereignty|sovereignty]], so it cannot force a member to change its domestic laws. Its members have more than 680 million people and a purchasing power parity-adjusted gross domestic product of around 6.3 percent of world GDP. Projects include the ASEAN Free Trade Area and the ASEAN Power Grid, and it organizes the SEA Games every two years. Its headquarters are in [[Jakarta]]. In the 2020s it has faced civil war in [[Myanmar]], territorial disputes in the [[South China Sea]] and tensions between the United States and China.

Dutch multinational company that makes [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] photolithography machines. ASML is the largest supplier to the [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] industry and the only maker of the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines needed for the most advanced chips. It was founded in 1984 as a joint venture of [[Philips]] and ASM International and became independent four years later. In 2012 [[Intel]] invested $4.1 billion for a 15 percent stake to help fund EUV development, and [[TSMC]] and Samsung later took smaller stakes. The governments of the Netherlands and the United States have restricted ASML's sales to [[China]].

American multinational [[Telecommunications|telecommunications]] holding company headquartered in [[Dallas]], Texas. The name abbreviates American Telephone and Telegraph Company, formed in 1885 as a long-distance subsidiary. Bell Telephone had been co-founded in 1877 by [[Alexander Graham Bell]]. For much of the 20th century AT&T was a regulated monopoly in U.S. telephony, nicknamed 'Ma Bell'. A 1982 antitrust settlement broke up the Bell System into seven companies. In 2005 SBC Communications bought AT&T Corporation and adopted its name. The company later sold DirecTV and merged WarnerMedia with Discovery, refocusing on 5G and fiber networks. AT&T has more than 240 million subscribers worldwide.

Indian spiritual teacher who founded the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON). Born in [[Kolkata]] as Abhay Charan De, he followed [[Vaishnavism|Vaishnava]] teachings. In 1965 he sailed to New York City on a [[Cargo ship|cargo ship]] to fulfill his teacher's instruction to spread Krishna consciousness in English, and in 1966 he established ISKCON there. He taught devotion to [[Krishna]] and chanting the Hare Krishna [[Mantra|mantra]], and required initiated students to abstain from meat, gambling, intoxicants and extramarital sex. His English translations of the *Bhagavad-gītā As It Is* and the *Srimad-Bhagavatam* made these texts widely accessible, and he wrote more than 80 books. Critics in America and Europe labeled ISKCON a destructive [[Cult|cult]] in the 1970s and 1980s, but scholars and courts rejected claims of brainwashing. Some critics have called his views racist, discriminatory against lower castes or misogynistic.

Novella by [[Charles Dickens]], published in London in 1843. It follows the elderly miser [[Ebenezer Scrooge|Scrooge]], who is visited on Christmas Eve by the ghost of his former partner Jacob Marley and by three spirits, and is transformed into a generous man. Dickens wrote it during the early Victorian revival of Christmas, after a visit to a London school for street children, and its themes include the treatment of the poor and the redemption of a selfish man. The first edition sold out by Christmas Eve. Dickens later gave public readings of the story, and it has been adapted many times for film, stage and opera.

1971 dystopian crime film directed by [[Stanley Kubrick]], adapted from Anthony Burgess's 1962 novel. It follows Alex, a violent delinquent played by [[Malcolm McDowell]], who undergoes an experimental aversion therapy called the Ludovico Technique. Alex narrates in Nadsat, an invented slang. The film's graphic violence made it controversial, and after it was linked to copycat crimes, Kubrick had it withdrawn from British cinemas. It received four Academy Award nominations, including Best Picture, and gained a cult following. In 2020 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the United States National Film Registry.

Three-act play by Norwegian playwright [[Henrik Ibsen]], first performed at the Royal Danish Theatre in [[Copenhagen]] on December 20, 1879. Set in a Norwegian town, it concerns Nora Helmer, a wife who secretly borrowed money to fund her husband Torvald's recovery from illness. When Torvald's response puts his reputation first, Nora leaves him and their three children. Ibsen denied that he intended a feminist play, but it caused an outcry in newspapers and society. In 2006 it was the world's most performed play. [[UNESCO]] inscribed Ibsen's autographed manuscripts on its Memory of the World Register in 2001.

English historian of 19th- and 20th-century European diplomacy. Taylor was a journalist and broadcaster, widely known through unscripted [[BBC]] television lectures on history, including *The War Lords* (1976) and *How Wars Begin* (1977). He lectured in history at the Victoria University of Manchester from 1930 to 1938 and was a fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, from 1938 to 1976. His 1961 book *The Origins of the Second World War* argued that [[Adolf Hitler]] did not follow a premeditated plan for conquest but exploited diplomatic errors by other powers. The argument sparked lasting debate among historians over intention and contingency. Other works include *The Struggle for Mastery in Europe, 1848–1918* (1954).

Comedy by [[William Shakespeare]], written about 1594–96. Set in [[Athens]] and a nearby forest, it interweaves three plots: the wedding of Duke Theseus and Hippolyta; the romances of four Athenian lovers, complicated by the [[Fairy|fairies]] of the forest; and a group of amateur actors, the mechanicals, rehearsing a play for the wedding. In the fairy plot, King Oberon and Queen Titania quarrel over an Indian changeling boy, and the mischievous sprite Puck applies a love potion that causes confusion. The play draws on [[Ovid]]'s *Metamorphoses* and is one of Shakespeare's most popular and frequently performed plays. It was first printed in a quarto edition in 1600.

Indian aerospace engineer and president of India from 2002 to 2007. Kalam worked at the [[ISRO|Indian Space Research Organisation]] and the Defence Research and Development Organisation, where he led work on satellite launch vehicles and ballistic missiles, earning the nickname 'Missile Man of India'. He played a key technical role in the 1998 Pokhran-II nuclear tests. He was elected president with the support of both the [[Bharatiya Janata Party]] and the [[Indian National Congress]]. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1997 and wrote books, including *Wings of Fire*, and promoted youth empowerment and technological innovation.

Indian composer, record producer and singer known for film music in Tamil and Hindi. Rahman's film career began in the early 1990s with the Tamil film *Roja*. His score for *Slumdog Millionaire* (2008) won two [[Academy Awards]], for best original score and for the song 'Jai Ho'. He won two [[Grammy Awards]] in 2010 and has received seven National Film Awards. Blending Indian classical music with electronic and orchestral sounds, he founded a music conservatory in [[Chennai]]. The Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan in 2010.

headword: A Song of Ice and Fire
entry: Series of high fantasy novels by American author [[George R. R. Martin]]. Set in the fictional continents of Westeros and Essos, it depicts a violent world dominated by political realism. Its three intertwined plots are a dynastic war for the Iron Throne, the attempt by the exiled Targaryen dynasty to return, and the threat posed by supernatural Others. Five of the planned seven volumes have been published, the latest being *A Dance with Dragons* (2011). The sixth, *The Winds of Winter*, remains unpublished. The novels have sold more than 100 million copies in 47 languages and inspired the [[HBO]] series *Game of Thrones*.

1947 play by [[Tennessee Williams]], first performed on Broadway on December 3, 1947. It follows Blanche DuBois, a former Southern belle who loses the family plantation and moves to the [[New Orleans]] apartment of her sister Stella and brother-in-law Stanley Kowalski. Blanche's evasions and fragility clash with Stanley's rough, domineering manner, and the play ends with her institutionalization. It won the 1948 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. [[Elia Kazan]] directed the premiere and the 1951 film, which earned [[Academy Awards]] for [[Vivien Leigh]] and [[Marlon Brando]].

headword: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
sort_key: sunday afternoon on the island of la grande jatte
entry: Painting by [[Georges Seurat]], made from 1884 to 1886 and his best-known work. It shows [[Paris|Parisians]] relaxing in a park on the island of La Grande Jatte in the Seine, at the edge of the city. The canvas, about 2 by 3 m, is a leading example of pointillism: small dots of pure color blend in the viewer's eye to produce brighter tones than conventional brushwork. Seurat preferred the term Divisionism for the method. The painting was first exhibited at the eighth and last Impressionist exhibition in 1886, establishing Seurat as the leader of Neo-Impressionism. It is held by the Art Institute of Chicago.

Historical novel by [[Charles Dickens]], published in 1859. Set in [[London]] and [[Paris]] before and during the [[French Revolution]], it follows Dr. Alexandre Manette, released after 18 years' imprisonment in the Bastille, and his daughter Lucie. Its plot centers on Charles Darnay, a French émigré tried for treason in London, and the dissolute lawyer Sydney Carton, who resembles him. The story covers the conditions that led to the French Revolution and the [[Reign of Terror|Reign of Terror]]. Serialized weekly in Dickens's journal *All the Year Round*, it is said to be one of the best-selling novels of all time. It ranked 63rd in the [[BBC]]'s *The Big Read* poll in 2003.
